To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) The extent of sublethally-inflicted damage in a tumour may differ from that in a related tumour; and 2) the extent of such differences in sublethally inflicted damage may be a major factor in determining differences in response of the two tumours to radiation of different LET.

(i) there are two closely-related rat tumours that differ markedly in their response to cyclotrons neutrons relative to low LET irradiations, (ii) these two tumours have the same structure and histology, (iii) the difference in neutron sensitivity is plausibly attributable to the extent of sub-lethal damage that the two tumour types shed between dose fractions, and (iv) the two tumour lines are not distinguishable on any of the usual criteria of hypoxic cell

In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of new techniques in radiotherapy, and we believe that it would be a great pity if the development of new methods of treatment should be retarded by the lack of a suitable method of selecting patients for clinical trials.

the development of a method for selecting patients with tumours that are likely to be more radiosensitive than average, and with the development of techniques for the clinical measurement of hypoxia and the extent of sub-lethal damage, and of the extent of the shoulder of the radiation dose-survival curve.

the identification of tumour cell populations that are resistant to radiation because they are either hypoxic, or because they shed a large proportion of their sublethal damage between dose fractions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no way of predicting which of two tumours is likely to be more sensitive to a given dose of radiation.

the two tumours differed in respect of their responses to neutrons and low LET radiation, that this was a difference of a kind that could be accounted for by differences in their responses to sublethal damage, and that the difference in response to sublethal was not related to any of the histological or structural differences that could be detected.

the differences in response to neutron radiation between the two pairs of rat tumour lines are explicable in terms of the differences in their response to low LET radiation, and that the differences in the response to low LET irradiation are not explicable in terms in terms of the histology and structure of the tumours.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the results of our experiments on tumour lines, and on human tumours in culture, are consistent with the view that hypoxia may be the major cause of the relative ineffectiveness of neutrons, but that sublethal damage may be the major factor responsible for the relative ineffectivenss of protracted irradiation.
it is possible to select patients with the probability of benefit from new radiotherapeutic methods that are based on radiobiological principles.

we are not in a position at present to make any useful predictions of the outcome of a clinical trial of a new radiotherapeutic technique in any given patient; but that the outcome of the trial may depend on the patient's tumour type and on the tumour's response to irradiation in terms of cell killing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of the RBE concept to compare the relative efficacy of different radiation qualities in clinical practice is not straightforward.
the combination of a hypoxia-targeted drug, such as tirapazamine, and a radiation dose escalation, can improve local tumor control and survival.
the combination of hypoxia and high LET radiation is more lethal than the same dose of high LET radiation alone.
